docs.title: Signing in through an organisation
docs.text:
Once a tenant declares an upstream identity provider, the people of its domains sign in there and nowhere else. The person who arrives at the login page is sent to the identity provider of their organisation, signs in as they do every morning, and comes back to the client or to the page that was waiting, as a person of the tenant.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant P as Beffroi
    participant I as Identity provider of the organisation
    B->>P: The login page asks for the address
    B->>P: alice@example.org
    P->>B: A signed AuthnRequest, to the provider of example.org
    B->>I: The person signs in there
    I->>B: A signed Response
    B->>P: POST /saml/sp/acs
    P->>B: The interaction goes on, a code goes to the client

docs.title: The login page asks for the address first
docs.text:
When the tenant has an upstream identity provider, the login page of an interaction shows one field, the address, and nothing else: no password, no passkey, no passkey offered by the browser's autofill. The same holds for the login a page of the provider asks for on its own, the approval of a device, a request waiting for an answer, the pages of the account or the single sign-on of a service provider. A tenant without an upstream identity provider shows the usual page.

The field is posted to /login/address, and what was typed decides where the browser goes:

What was typed Where the browser goes An address of a domain an identity provider answers for To the sign-on of that identity provider, /saml/sp/sign-on, by a 303, which sends it on to the provider An address of any other domain Back to the usual login page, its username field holding what was typed, with a way back to the address A value without an @ The same: a username, of no domain An address whose domain cannot be read Back to the page of the address, which says so

The domain is read one way everywhere it is read: the whole part after the last @, through the IDNA of UTS #46 into its A-label, lower-cased, so an address typed in capitals, in Unicode or in its A-label belongs to the same domain.

Nothing here reads a person. The answer depends on the domain and on the declarations of the tenant, and on nothing else: the page answers the same status, the same headers and the same body whether somebody holds that address or not, and waits on no lookup a clock could tell apart. The field holds what this browser typed last, or the login_hint of the request when it is an address, as the client wrote it.

A login_hint of a federated domain skips the page. When the authorization request carries a login_hint (OIDC Core §3.1.2.1) that is an address of a domain an identity provider answers for, the login page sends the browser to that provider at once and shows nothing. Every later render of that login goes there again: such an interaction is signed in through the identity provider or not at all.

docs.title: The request sent upstream
docs.text:
The sign-on starts at /saml/sp/sign-on, and only from the login page: the redirection that sends the browser there carries a reference drawn for that login and kept in the session of that browser, used once and valid one minute. A sign-on that presents no reference, or one this browser was not given, writes no request: a page of another site can send a browser to that route but cannot read its session, so nobody can start the login of a person who did not ask for one and have it answered by a session held elsewhere.

The request is an AuthnRequest written and signed by the SAML key of the tenant:

What Value Where it goes The first single sign-on service of the accepted metadata on HTTP-Redirect, or on HTTP-POST when the provider offers no other, never an address a request or a page names Signature RSA-SHA256, over the query string for HTTP-Redirect, in the XML for HTTP-POST Issuer The entity ID of the service provider of the tenant AssertionConsumerServiceURL /saml/sp/acs, with the HTTP-POST binding NameIDPolicy persistent, with AllowCreate="true" ForceAuthn When the client asked for a login the session of this browser cannot answer, and when a page asks a signed-in person for a fresh proof RelayState 32 random bytes in base64url, and nothing else: no URL, no value of the request

ForceAuthn follows what the login page itself would ask of a browser that holds a session of the provider: prompt=login, a max_age that session exceeds, a step-up, prompt=select_account, an id_token_hint naming another person. A browser that holds no session forces a login for prompt=login alone, and the age of what the person proved is checked when the response comes back. Without it, a session the person left open at their identity provider would answer a client that asked for a fresh login.

The request is remembered in the HTTP session of the browser, under its RelayState, for ten minutes, eight at most per browser: what a response answers is read there, and nowhere else.

The address can go with it. An identity provider that reads a hint on its sign-in page is declared with address_parameter, login_hint for Microsoft Entra ID, and the address typed on the login page, or the login_hint that skipped it, is added in that parameter: after the Signature over HTTP-Redirect, outside what is signed, and in the query of the form's action over HTTP-POST. It goes only to the provider that answers for its domain, and it is a hint and never a proof: the person is who the signed assertion names, whatever the form at the provider was prefilled with.

docs.title: The response taken back
docs.text:
The assertion consumer service is /saml/sp/acs, POST only, a body in application/x-www-form-urlencoded and nothing else (415). The identity provider posts it from its own site, so it arrives without the session cookie, and it is posted again once from the provider's own origin, as a sign-on request is.

A response nobody asked for is refused. The RelayState has to name a request this browser remembers, sent less than ten minutes ago, and it is forgotten as it is read, so a form posted twice finds nothing the second time. A response that answers no request this provider sent cannot be told apart from one an attacker obtained for their own account, which is how a victim gets signed in to the attacker's.

It is verified under the provider the request went to, never under one the message names: its InResponseTo is that request, its Issuer that provider, its Destination and Recipient the URL of the assertion consumer service, its Audience the entity ID of the service provider. Every assertion is covered by a signature, its own or the response's, made by a key of the provider's metadata, and is accepted once. An encrypted assertion is opened by the keys of that provider alone.

A response whose status is not Success carries no assertion and signs nobody in. The person cancelled or failed at their identity provider, so the client is answered access_denied at its redirection URI with its state, or login_required when the provider answered NoPassive to a request with prompt=none (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6), and nothing the identity provider wrote reaches the client.

Every refusal is a page that names the rule and never a value of the response, opens no session and writes nothing of the person. A response the service provider does not take, a person it may not sign in and a login under the floor of the tenant are each written to the journal as a refused login, with the method fed.

docs.title: The person
docs.text:
Named by the provider, never by an address. The subject is the value of a persistent NameID, or, for a provider declared with subject_attribute, the one value of that attribute. A subject that is the same mailbox as the address of the assertion is refused whatever names it, so a mailbox given to somebody new never leads to the account of the one who held it.

Found by the link, never by the address. The person is the one whose linked identity names that provider and that subject. At the first sign-in there is none, and the person is created in one unit, all of it kept or none of it:

  • the person, its subject drawn as any other, its username its address, the address verified, the provider answering for its domain;
  • its source, the identity provider, with the claims of the profile it filled;
  • its linked identity, with what the provider said;
  • a telephone number, unverified, when the profile maps one;
  • its memberships, the groups the declaration maps the values of the groups attribute to.

The address has to be in a domain of that provider, and held by no other person of the tenant, as a mailbox or as a username: an existing account is never linked on its own. An administrator who wants a person who already exists to sign in through a provider links them by hand, naming the entity ID of the provider and the subject it gives that person:

bin/console beffroi:user:link alice 'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata' 'the-subject-it-gives-alice'

A person linked that way signs in under the link with none of the rules of a first sign-in, only the snapshot of the linked identity being refreshed.

The provider keeps what it fills. At every later sign-in, what the source holds becomes exactly what the provider fills and says now, the memberships it asserts are replaced, and the username follows the address when the provider sends another one. A claim it no longer says is released to the person, with the value it wrote last. What the source holds, neither the person on the page of their account nor an operator with beffroi:user:profile can change.

A disabled person is refused before anything of them is written: an account an administrator disabled keeps what it held and stops following the provider. The page says what it says of every refusal, and nothing of the state of the account.

docs.title: The session
docs.text:
What Value amr fed, a federated assertion, and the class of the provider where its meaning is exactly a method (RFC 8176 §2): Password and PasswordProtectedTransport add pwd, Smartcard adds sc, TimeSyncToken adds otp, any other class adds nothing auth_time The AuthnInstant of the assertion, the instant the person authenticated at their provider, never the instant the response arrived Its end No later than the SessionNotOnOrAfter the provider set, which is the one way it has of ending the session it vouches for. An assertion whose SessionNotOnOrAfter has passed is refused

The session is opened under the floor of the tenant, like every login: a tenant that asks for two factors refuses a login that proved fed and pwd alone.

What the client asked is held at the response. A login made during the interaction, an AuthnInstant at or after the instant it began, satisfies prompt=login, a max_age and a step-up. An earlier one does not: the request is sent once more with ForceAuthn when the first one did not carry it, and when it did, the client is answered login_required, or account_selection_required for prompt=select_account. A request is never sent a third time, so a provider that ignores ForceAuthn never sends the browser round without end. The comparison has no tolerance for clocks, and a provider whose clock lags by more than the time a person takes to sign in answers login_required until its clock is set.

The browser goes back to what was waiting, and nowhere a response or a parameter names: the login page of the interaction, which resumes it and sends the code to the redirection URI the client registered, or the page of the provider that asked for the login.

docs.title: No local credential for an organisation's people
docs.text:
A person whose address is of a domain an identity provider answers for, their mailbox or a username holding an @, signs in through that provider and through nothing else.

  • At the login, a password, a passkey and the code that completes a password are refused for them, whatever the page offered, so a form written by hand fails as the page would. A refused password answers as a wrong one, at the cost of a wrong one, and the journal records why.
  • On the pages of the account, no form that would pose a password, a passkey or an authenticator application is offered, and the page says why: their organisation signs them in.
  • Anywhere a credential is posed, the console setting a password, an enrolment ticket for a passkey, a TOTP, a renewal of backup codes, the replacement of a password held before the domain was federated: the answer is the same refusal.

So a person who leaves the organisation and loses their account in its directory has no local password left that outlives the departure.

On a tenant with an upstream identity provider, an address whose domain cannot be read counts as one of a federated domain, refused rather than taken for an address of none. The account an administrator keeps for the day the identity provider is down therefore has a username without an @, or an address in a domain of two labels at least that no provider declares, and never one such as admin@localhost.

docs.title: The identity provider
docs.text: The tenant is the SAML identity provider of the service providers it declares: they send it an AuthnRequest, and it answers with a signed assertion about the person signed in. This page is the role itself, its key and the document that describes it. Service providers is how one is declared, and single sign-on what a request gets.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        identity_provider:
            enabled: true
Option Default What it decides enabled false Whether the role exists at all. Off, its metadata answer 404, no service provider may be declared, and every message at its single sign-on and single logout services is refused want_authn_requests_signed true What the metadata say in WantAuthnRequestsSigned (SAML Metadata §2.4.3) staging_delay 604800, seven days How long a new SAML signing key is published in the metadata before it signs, in seconds age 31536000, 365 days How long a SAML signing key works before a successor is staged behind it, in seconds, counted from its activation cache_duration 86400, one day The cacheDuration of the metadata (SAML Metadata §2.3.2), in seconds: how long a service provider keeps them before it fetches them again. One second at least, and strictly shorter than staging_delay, which the configuration refuses otherwise

The three figures belong to the deployment and not to a tenant, as those of beffroi.keys do, and they are the figures of the SAML key whichever role draws it: the service provider of the tenant signs with the same key.

want_authn_requests_signed is an announcement, and nothing more. It tells a service provider configured from the metadata to sign its requests, which is what a broker such as SimpleSAMLphp does when it reads true. Whether a request that arrives needs a signature is decided per service provider, by its declaration and its own metadata, and the setting neither adds a signature to that rule nor takes one from it: the signature a request needs says how.

docs.title: The key
docs.text:
The SAML signing key is a key of the tenant like every other one. Its algorithm is SAML-SIGNING, an RSA key of 3072 bits, the size every RSA key of the tenant is drawn at. The key pair is drawn in the process, its private half sealed by the key management service before anything is written, and opened in memory when the process signs. It is not in the JWK Set and it is not in the metadata: what the metadata publish is a certificate around its public half.

Turning a role on does not draw a key. On a deployment that has none, draw it once:

bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING

From then on it lives the life of every key of the tenant, with the same commands: beffroi:keys:rotate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING stages a successor, beffroi:keys:activate brings a staged key in before its date, beffroi:keys:retire takes a retiring one out, and the timed step stages a successor on its own once the active key has worked its age. A tenant with no SAML key in service has no metadata, and answers 404 there until it has one.

A deployment that turns both roles off after its tenant drew a key leaves that key where it is: nothing serves it, rotates it or draws it again, and turning a role back on puts it back in service as it was.

Keys, and the commands that rotate them

docs.title: The certificate
docs.text:
A service provider identifies the key of an identity provider by an X.509 certificate, so each SAML key in service is published inside one. It is the key's own: self-signed by that key, and verified under the public half it carries before it is published.

Field Value Subject and issuer CN= the slug of the tenant Validity Ten years from the creation of the key, written as UTCTime Extensions keyUsage with digitalSignature alone, critical Signature sha256WithRSAEncryption, by the key itself

Its bytes are a function of the key and of the tenant, so every process of the deployment publishes the same certificate for the same key. The ten years are not how long the key works: the key signs for its age, one year by default, and its status is what retires it. A certificate in metadata is how a key is written down, and a service provider that follows the SAML V2.0 Metadata Interoperability Profile does not evaluate its validity period (§2.6.1). Ten years is what hosted identity providers issue theirs for, and Microsoft Entra ID refused a certificate valid until the year 9999, written in the GeneralizedTime RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 gives a certificate that never expires, whether for the date or for its encoding.

docs.title: The metadata
docs.text:
The metadata are served at /saml/metadata, and that URL is the entity ID of the identity provider: a service provider resolves an entity ID to its metadata there (SAML Metadata §4.1), and keeps it. Changing the issuer of a deployment is therefore a new identity provider for every service provider that knew the old one.

https://op.example.com/saml/metadata

What they hold is read from the configuration of the tenant, never from the request that asked for them:

  • one md:EntityDescriptor holding one md:IDPSSODescriptor of SAML 2.0;
  • one KeyDescriptor use="signing" per SAML key in service, staged, active and retiring, in the order they were created;
  • the single sign-on service at /saml/sso and the single logout service at /saml/slo, each listed with HTTP-Redirect and then HTTP-POST at the same URL;
  • WantAuthnRequestsSigned, as the configuration says;
  • one NameIDFormat, urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:persistent, the only format the identity provider writes;
  • the cacheDuration of the configuration, and no validUntil.

They carry no encryption certificate, since the identity provider decrypts nothing a service provider sends it, and they are not signed: the key that would sign them is the key they publish, so a service provider trusts them by the channel it read them through, the URL over TLS or the file an administrator gave it. They are served as application/samlmetadata+xml, with Cache-Control: public and the max-age of the JWK Set, five minutes unless beffroi.keys.jwks_max_age says otherwise, so a cache on the way never holds a copy older than that.

The routes have to be mounted under the issuer, as the discovery document's are: the bundle refuses to write metadata whose endpoints would not be.

docs.title: A rotation without an outage
docs.text:
A service provider that pinned the old certificate refuses everything the new key signs, so the next certificate is published long before it is used.

graph LR
  s["staged<br/><small>in the metadata,<br/>signs nothing</small>"] -- "seven days" --> a["active<br/><small>signs</small>"]
  a -- "its successor,<br/>staged at 365 days,<br/>takes over" --> r["retiring<br/><small>still in the metadata</small>"]
  r --> x["retired"]

Staged for seven days. A rotation adds the certificate of the next key to the metadata a week before that key signs anything. A service provider that honours the cacheDuration of one day fetches the metadata seven times in that week, so six refreshes may fail, a job that did not run over a weekend among them, and it still takes the next certificate before that key signs.

A week is also what a person needs. A service provider whose administrator uploaded the certificate by hand, rather than pointing it at the metadata, has the staging window to put the next one in place. beffroi:keys:list shows the date the staged key takes over, and beffroi:keys:activate moves it to the minute the administrator chooses.

A year of work. Every rotation is a step for whoever pinned a certificate, so a successor is staged behind the SAML key once it has worked 365 days, and takes over a week later. A year is inside the one to three years NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 §5.3.6 gives a private signature key, where the other keys of the tenant work ninety days. Those keep the figures of beffroi.keys, and a rotation of one of them is not slowed by the SAML key.

The key management service is not asked at every login: a process opens the active key once to sign and keeps it open, as it does the keys that sign tokens.

docs.title: Microsoft Entra ID
docs.text: Entra ID meets Beffroi in both directions. It can federate the guests of a Microsoft tenant to Beffroi, which is then their identity provider; and an enterprise application of Entra can be the upstream identity provider of a tenant of Beffroi, for the people of the domains it answers for. Both have been played against a Microsoft tenant, and what Entra needs that its documentation does not say is built into the provider rather than left to a setting.

docs.title: Entra federating its guests to Beffroi
docs.text: Here Entra is a service provider of the tenant: a guest of the Microsoft tenant is sent to Beffroi to sign in, through the SAML/WS-Fed identity provider federation of Entra External ID.

docs.title: The service provider Entra is
docs.text:
Entra publishes no metadata for this federation, so they are written by hand, from what Microsoft documents, and declared as a file of the deployment.

config/saml/entra-guest-federation-sp.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<md:EntityDescriptor xmlns:md="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata"
    entityID="https://login.microsoftonline.com/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/">
  <md:SPSSODescriptor protocolSupportEnumeration="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol">
    <md:NameIDFormat>urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:persistent</md:NameIDFormat>
    <md:AssertionConsumerService Binding="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:bindings:HTTP-POST"
        Location="https://login.microsoftonline.com/login.srf" index="0" isDefault="true"/>
  </md:SPSSODescriptor>
</md:EntityDescriptor>
What Why The entity ID is https://login.microsoftonline.com/ followed by the ID of the Microsoft tenant and a slash It is the Issuer of the requests Entra sends for a new federation, and the Audience it expects; the final slash is part of it One assertion consumer service, login.srf, on HTTP-POST Where Entra receives the response No key Entra does not sign the requests of this federation No single logout service Nothing documents single logout for it, and a service listed is one a LogoutRequest would be sent to config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        identity_provider: true
        service_providers:
            'https://login.microsoftonline.com/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/':
                metadata: '%kernel.project_dir%/config/saml/entra-guest-federation-sp.xml'
                signs_authn_requests: false
                attributes:
                    'http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2005/05/identity/claims/emailaddress':
                        claim: email

signs_authn_requests: false is what lets an unsigned request in, from this service provider and no other. The one attribute Entra requires is the e-mail address of the guest, under its claim type. Then read the metadata:

bin/console beffroi:saml:service-provider:refresh

docs.title: What the Entra portal takes
docs.text: Field of the portal What to give it Issuer URI The entity ID of the identity provider of the tenant, https://op.example.com/saml/metadata Passive authentication endpoint Its single sign-on service, https://op.example.com/saml/sso Signing certificate The base64 of the certificate of the active SAML key, as the metadata publish it Metadata URL Optional. Microsoft's service reads it, so a provider Microsoft cannot reach offers none

docs.title: What Entra asks that it does not document
docs.text:
Each is how the provider behaves for every service provider, with no setting to turn it off:

  • Every signature carries the certificate. A response whose signatures carry no KeyInfo is refused by Entra with AADSTS5000810: Unable to verify token signature. Signing key identifier is missing.
  • The Conditions carry a NotBefore. An assertion without one is refused with AADSTS500089.
  • The certificate expires. The portal refused a certificate valid until the year 9999, written in GeneralizedTime, whether for the date or for its encoding; the one around the SAML key is valid ten years, written in UTCTime.
  • The request is posted from Entra's site, unsigned, with a RelayState of several hundred bytes: it is posted again from the provider's own origin, so the session cookie comes with it, and its RelayState is given back as it came.
  • The page that posts the response names no form-action, since login.srf sends the browser on to the client that asked Entra, an origin nothing declares.

docs.title: A rotation of the SAML key
docs.text:
The federation holds one signing certificate. With a metadata URL Microsoft can reach, Entra renews it when it is about to expire; at a rotation it does not, and the certificate is replaced by hand, at the moment the next key takes over, since the old certificate stops verifying the minute the new key signs.

That moment is known a week ahead: beffroi:keys:list shows when the staged SAML key activates, and beffroi:keys:activate moves the take-over to the minute the administrator of the Microsoft tenant chooses.

docs.title: Entra ID as an upstream identity provider
docs.text: Here Entra is the identity provider of an organisation, and the tenant of Beffroi is its service provider: a person of the organisation's domain types their address on the login page and signs in at Microsoft.

docs.title: In the Entra portal
docs.text:
An enterprise application with SAML single sign-on:

Field Value Identifier (Entity ID) The entity ID of the service provider of the tenant, https://op.example.com/saml/sp/metadata Reply URL (Assertion Consumer Service URL) https://op.example.com/saml/sp/acs Signing option Sign the SAML response and the assertion, under SHA-256

The Federation Metadata XML of the application is what the tenant reads. Its entity ID is https://sts.windows.net/ followed by the ID of the Microsoft tenant and a slash. It is signed but carries no validUntil, which metadata verified under pinned signers must carry, so it is trusted by the channel it came through and metadata_signers stays empty. A certificate rolled over in the portal is a new document to read.

docs.title: The declaration
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        service_provider: true
        identity_providers:
            'https://sts.windows.net/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/':
                metadata: '%kernel.project_dir%/config/saml/entra-idp.xml'
                domains: ['example.org']
                email_attribute: 'http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2005/05/identity/claims/emailaddress'
                subject_attribute: 'http://schemas.microsoft.com/identity/claims/objectidentifier'
                profile:
                    'http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2005/05/identity/claims/givenname': given_name
                    'http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2005/05/identity/claims/surname': family_name
                groups:
                    attribute: 'http://schemas.microsoft.com/ws/2008/06/identity/claims/groups'
                    map:
                        '11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111': finance
                address_parameter: login_hint
Option Why this value domains The domain of the addresses of the organisation's people email_attribute The claim type Entra sends the user's mail under. Every attribute is named by its claim type, the URI, and not by the short name the portal shows subject_attribute The request asks for a persistent NameID, which Entra answers with an identifier of the person for this application: that is the subject. Should the application be set to send its NameID in another format, the e-mail address its portal offers among them, the object ID of the user, a value that does not change, names the person instead. A persistent NameID whose value is the address of the person is refused groups Entra sends security groups as their object IDs, which a group renamed in the portal does not change, so the map is keyed by object ID address_parameter Entra reads login_hint on its sign-in URL and prefills its form with it, so the person types their address once

Create the groups the map names, then read the metadata:

bin/console beffroi:group:create finance
bin/console beffroi:saml:identity-provider:refresh

docs.title: The SAML packages
docs.text:
XML Signature and XML Encryption are the two specifications where a permissive reader becomes a vulnerability: signature wrapping, entity expansion, a canonicalization that does not cover what the verifier thinks it covers. So the format is written here, in three libraries with no SAML or XML Signature library underneath, each held to a written specification of its own, and the profile the tenants use sits on top of them.

Package Namespace What it holds Requires beffroi/xml-security Beffroi\Xml Core, a safe DOM; Dsig, XML Signature; Enc, XML Encryption PHP 8.4, ext-dom, ext-libxml, ext-openssl beffroi/saml2-model Beffroi\Saml2\Model The samlp:, saml: and md: objects of Web Browser SSO and Single Logout, read strictly, validated and written. No HTTP xml-security, psr/clock beffroi/saml2-bindings Beffroi\Saml2\Bindings HTTP-Redirect and HTTP-POST, on strings and arrays, never on an HTTP object saml2-model, xml-security, ext-zlib beffroi/saml Beffroi\Saml The profile for the tenants: the identity provider and the service provider of a tenant, their metadata, the attributes, the NameID, single logout on the session of the core the three above, beffroi/core, spomky-labs/pki-framework, ext-intl 
graph RL
  saml["beffroi/saml"] --> bindings["saml2-bindings"]
  saml --> model["saml2-model"]
  saml --> xml["xml-security"]
  saml --> core["beffroi/core"]
  bindings --> model
  bindings --> xml
  model --> xml

The first three know nothing of Beffroi and are usable by any PHP project that speaks SAML. Each rule they state is code, never an option, and each refusal names the rule it applies and never a value of the input, so a message can be logged without what it carried.

docs.title: xml-security
docs.text:
Core loads XML without being attacked. It takes bytes, never a path or a stream, and refuses, before anything reads the tree: a document type declaration anywhere in the bytes, an encoding other than UTF-8, an XML version other than 1.0, any diagnostic of libxml at any level, and an input past its bounds.

Bound Default Size 1 MiB Depth 64 Elements 10 000 Attributes per element 32 Namespace declarations 512 Length of an identifier 128 bytes

A document has one space of identifiers, built at load, in which a duplicate is refused, and an element is found by identifier through that index, never by XPath and never by searching descendants. Text is the concatenation of the text and CDATA children, comments skipped, so user@example.com<!---->.evil.com reads as user@example.com.evil.com, the value the signature covers. Canonicalization knows the four methods of Canonical XML 1.0 and Exclusive XML Canonicalization 1.0, with and without comments, and nothing ever canonicalizes to the empty string.

Dsig verifies only what the signature covers. One reference, to the element that claims to be signed; the enveloped signature and exclusive canonicalization transforms and no others; RSA with SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, and RSASSA-PSS where PHP 8.5 and OpenSSL 3.1 provide it; RSA keys of 2048 bits at least. SHA-1, MD5, HMAC, DSA, ECDSA, XPath and XSLT are refused before anything is computed. The key is the one the consumer gives, never one the KeyInfo of the signature names, and what the consumer reads afterwards is the bytes that were hashed, loaded again.

Enc builds no oracle. It writes AES-GCM, under RSA-OAEP, with fresh randomness for every message. It reads AES-CBC only under a signature that covers the ciphertext and never writes it, and every cryptographic failure is one and the same refusal, so a padding error, a wrong key and a broken tag cannot be told apart.

docs.title: saml2-model
docs.text:
The model reads an assertion only in what a signature covers, takes a peer's keys from its metadata only, and knows no HTTP.

use Beffroi\Saml2\Model\Protocol\UnverifiedResponse;
use Beffroi\Saml2\Model\SamlLoader;
use Beffroi\Saml2\Model\Validation\{ExpectedResponse, ResponseValidator, TimeBounds};

$loader = SamlLoader::create();                              // one loader, one ID space for SAML, ds: and xenc:
$response = UnverifiedResponse::of($loader->load($bytes));   // the bytes a binding decoded
$idp = $peers->identityProvider($response->issuer);          // the unverified issuer chooses the peer, nothing else

$accepted = new ResponseValidator($loader, $clock, $replayGuard, new TimeBounds())->validate(
    $response,
    $idp,
    ExpectedResponse::toRequest($requestId, 'https://sp.example.com/saml/acs', 'https://sp.example.com/saml'),
);
$accepted->assertion->nameId->value;                         // read from the verified document only

validate() refuses with an exception that names its rule, SignatureRequired, AudienceMismatch, OutsideValidityWindow, Replayed and the others. The other messages of the two profiles have their writer and their validator: AuthnRequestWriter and AuthnRequestValidator, ResponseWriter, LogoutRequestWriter and LogoutRequestValidator, LogoutResponseWriter and LogoutResponseValidator, and MetadataReader and MetadataWriter for the metadata.

The model guarantees M-1 What is read is what was verified, or what was decrypted from a ciphertext that was M-2 Every assertion is covered by a signature, its own or the response's, and every signature present verifies M-3 A peer's keys come from its metadata; the KeyInfo of a message is never read M-4 One assertion per response, found as a direct child; one subject, one bearer confirmation M-5 The order and cardinality of the schema are code; a closed vocabulary refuses what it does not know M-6 One lexical form per value: UTC times, booleans never cast, absolute URIs of 1024 characters at most M-7 Time comes from a PSR-20 clock, and every window has a bounded skew M-8 Issuer, Audience, Recipient and Destination are compared byte for byte M-9 An assertion goes only to an assertion consumer service the metadata list M-10 InResponseTo answers the request the consumer names, or is absent when it accepts an unsolicited response M-11 An assertion, and a logout message, is accepted once M-12 A NameID follows the rules of its format, read whole M-13 A failure status, an unknown condition or an unsupported element is a refusal M-14 One loader and one space of identifiers for SAML, XML Signature and XML Encryption M-15 What it writes, it reads back under the same rules M-16 A refusal names its rule and never carries a value of the message M-17 Every count and length is bounded, and checked before anything iterates M-18 The consumer is told whether the assertion arrived encrypted

Two ports. The clock is PSR-20's ClockInterface. The replay port is one method, implemented over a store every worker of the deployment shares, atomically: a store per process forgets across workers.

namespace Beffroi\Saml2\Model\Port;

interface ReplayGuardInterface
{
    /** true when the pair was new and is now remembered until $expiresAt, false when it was seen */
    public function remember(string $issuer, string $id, \DateTimeImmutable $expiresAt): bool;
}

docs.title: saml2-bindings
docs.text:
The two browser bindings, on strings and arrays: a query string or the fields of a form decoded into the document the model reads, and a message the model writes turned into a URL or a form. It reads no SAML element itself; which message it expects is the method that is called.

use Beffroi\Saml2\Bindings\RedirectReceiver;
use Beffroi\Saml2\Model\SamlLoader;
use Beffroi\Saml2\Model\Validation\AuthnRequestValidator;

$loader = SamlLoader::create();
$received = new RedirectReceiver($loader)->authnRequest($queryString);   // the raw QUERY_STRING, as it arrived
$accepted = $received->validate(
    new AuthnRequestValidator($loader, $clock),
    $peers->serviceProvider($received->request->issuer),
    $self,
    'https://idp.example.com/saml/sso',                                  // the endpoint, from configuration
);
$received->relayState;                                                  // opaque, echoed in the answer
The bindings guarantee B-1 One message parameter, and every parameter at most once, under its literal name B-2 The HTTP-Redirect signature is verified over SAMLRequest or SAMLResponse, RelayState and SigAlg, in that order, as received B-3 Signature and SigAlg go together, SigAlg on the closed list of xml-security, SHA-1 and DSA refused B-4 The keys are those of the peer's metadata B-5 The model hears that the binding authenticated a message only from this package, after the signature held over the very input the message was decoded from B-6 No XML signature travels over HTTP-Redirect B-7 Every input is bounded before it is decoded, and DEFLATE while it inflates B-8 One lexical form: strict percent-encoding, canonical base64, raw DEFLATE complete and alone B-9 RelayState is opaque, 1024 bytes at most, never empty, and never given to the model B-10 What arrived is loaded as it arrived; what is sent is serialized once B-11 A refusal names its rule and never carries a value of the input B-12 No response over HTTP-Redirect, and every logout message sent is signed B-13 No HTTP object, no superglobal, no header, no HTML

Two deviations from SAML Bindings are deliberate, and neither is a switch: RSA-SHA1 and DSA-SHA1, which §3.4.4.1 requires, are refused; and a RelayState of up to 1024 bytes is read and sent where §3.4.3 and §3.5.3 say 80, since real service providers send longer ones.

What the application holds. The raw query string, never one a framework normalised; the fields of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body, any other content type refused before the call; the URL of its own endpoint from its configuration, never rebuilt from the Host of the request; the RelayState it draws, an unguessable reference to state it keeps; and the page that posts a form, every value escaped for HTML and the script that submits it allowed by the content security policy.

docs.title: What a consumer never calls
docs.text:
Each package is held by PHPStan rules of its own, kept in the monorepo beside its tests, which its consumers are asked to copy: the DOM classes, XPath, SimpleXML, XMLReader and XMLWriter outside the loader, the flags of libxml that load a DTD or expand an entity, getElementById(), the weak generators of randomness, a loose comparison and a cast to bool. Above them, beffroi/saml never calls the method by which the bindings tell the model a signature held, nor Reflection, Closure::bind() or the unserializer, any of which would let a message received over the binding be paired with a signature verified over another input. Its analysis proves each ban with a fixture, one line per banned form, so a rule that stops firing turns the build red.

The specification of each package is in its directory of the monorepo, beffroi-auth/beffroi, and each is published read only as a repository of its own.

docs.title: Service providers
docs.text: A service provider is an application that signs its users in through the identity provider of the tenant. It exists here because the deployment declares it, keyed by its entity ID as a client of OpenID Connect is keyed by its client_id. No request registers one and no page edits one: a peer that may obtain an assertion about anybody is a decision of whoever runs the deployment.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        identity_provider: true
        service_providers:
            'https://sp.example.com/saml/metadata':
                metadata: 'https://sp.example.com/saml/metadata'
                attributes:
                    'urn:oid:0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.1':
                        claim: preferred_username
                        friendly_name: uid
                    'urn:oid:0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.3':
                        claim: email
                        friendly_name: mail
                    'urn:oid:2.16.840.1.113730.3.1.241':
                        claim: name
                        friendly_name: displayName
Option Default What it decides The key The entity ID of the service provider, compared exactly with the one its metadata carry: at most 1024 characters, no whitespace metadata required Where its metadata are read from: an https URL, or the absolute path of a file of the deployment. Nothing else, a plain http URL included metadata_signers none The certificates the metadata are signed by, each the base64 of its DER as an X509Certificate carries it, sixteen at most. Named, the metadata are verified under them; left empty, they are trusted by the channel they come through attributes none The claims sent to this service provider, keyed by the name of the attribute each one is sent as, 256 at most encrypt_assertions false Its assertions are encrypted for a key of its metadata signs_authn_requests true It signs its authentication requests

A declaration is refused while the identity provider of the tenant is not enabled, and a declaration that does not hold together fails the build of the deployment rather than its first login: when the container is compiled for every rule, and right after it, in the same build, for the claims the attributes name. A declaration that holds an environment variable, whose value only the running deployment knows, is held to the same rules at its first use.

docs.title: Its metadata
docs.text:
The declaration says where the metadata are; what they say is read there, and nowhere else. They are where the assertion consumer services of the service provider are, its single logout services, and the keys its requests are verified with: the declaration names none of them, so a service provider cannot be sent an assertion anywhere its own metadata do not list.

Read before the first login. A service provider whose metadata have never been accepted is refused, so a declaration is followed by a reading:

bin/console beffroi:saml:service-provider:refresh
bin/console beffroi:saml:service-provider:refresh 'https://sp.example.com/saml/metadata'

Without an argument it reads every service provider the configuration declares. Each one is reported as registered, registered by another process meanwhile, refreshed, unchanged, refused or failed, and a refusal names the rule it broke and never a value of the document. A timed step does the same every hour, for the service providers and the upstream identity providers alike, and writes a refusal to the log as an error: the refused document comes back at every hour while the accepted one goes on serving, which is something an operator wants to be alerted on.

How they are fetched. A URL is fetched with one GET, no redirect followed, ten seconds at most, and any status but 2xx refused. A file or a body is refused as soon as it passes one mebibyte, which no metadata the loader accepts reaches.

What is refused, at the first reading as at every refresh, the accepted document being kept each time:

  • a document whose entity ID is not the declared one, or that holds no md:SPSSODescriptor of SAML 2.0;
  • a document past its validUntil, or past the validUntil of its service provider role;
  • an assertion consumer service or a single logout service that is not https on a host, with no userinfo;
  • metadata with no key for encryption, for a declaration that asks for encrypted assertions;
  • metadata with no key for signing, for a service provider whose requests need a signature;
  • a document read under pinned signers that carries no validUntil, or whose validUntil is earlier than the one of the document already accepted.

Endpoints on other bindings than HTTP-Redirect and HTTP-POST are dropped, an assertion consumer service on anything but HTTP-POST too, since no other binding the provider sends over can carry a response, and the other role descriptors are skipped, so that the metadata of a real deployment load.

Signed metadata never go back. An older document signed by the same key verifies as well as the newer one, so under pinned signers a document older than the accepted one is refused, which is the rollback the signature cannot catch by itself. Metadata trusted by their channel follow the channel instead: the next reading replaces the accepted document whatever its validUntil, so that a document planted while somebody else held the host gives way at the first refresh after the host is the service provider's again.

Only a person goes back on it. Forgetting the accepted document is a command run by hand, never a step of the schedule nor a request, and the next reading then registers the service provider as a first one:

bin/console beffroi:saml:service-provider:forget 'https://sp.example.com/saml/metadata'

An entity ID for which nothing is accepted is answered so, and the command fails, so a mistyped entity ID is never taken for a forgotten one. A declaration removed from the configuration leaves its accepted document where it is, read by nothing, until an operator forgets it.

Sealed where it sits. The document is kept as the bytes that were read and sealed under the data key of the tenant, since an md:ContactPerson names people.

docs.title: The attributes it receives
docs.text:
An assertion carries one Attribute per mapping whose claim the person holds, under the name, the name format and the friendly name the mapping gives, and nothing else. A claim may be sent under several names.

Key Default What it is claim required The name of the claim, as OpenID Connect names it (OIDC Core §5.1). The claims are the ones the provider serves to OpenID Connect, so a claim a deployment adds can be mapped the day its class is wired name_format uri The name format of the attribute (SAML Core §8.2): uri, under which the name is an absolute URI, as the SAML V2.0 interoperability profiles ask; basic; or unspecified friendly_name none A name a person reads (SAML Core §2.7.3.1), which nothing compares

A value is the text of the claim: a string as it is, an integer in decimal, a boolean as true or false, and a list as one value per member. A value holding a character XML 1.0 cannot carry, a control character other than the tab and the line breaks or bytes that are not UTF-8, is not sent, and neither is a claim that is an object, such as address. The refusal goes to the log, naming the service provider, the claim and the rule but never the value, and the sign-on goes on without that attribute: an attribute is the person's statement to that service provider, and one cut short or rewritten on the way would be a statement they never made.

docs.title: The signature a request needs
docs.text:
An AuthnRequest needs a signature, in its XML or over the query string of HTTP-Redirect, unless both the service provider and its metadata say it does not sign. Whichever of the two says it signs wins:

signs_authn_requests AuthnRequestsSigned of its metadata An unsigned request true, the default anything refused false true refused false false or absent accepted

Nothing else decides it, neither the WantAuthnRequestsSigned the identity provider announces nor any setting of the tenant or of the deployment. A signature a request does carry is verified whatever the rule says, under the keys of the metadata and never under a key the message names.

signs_authn_requests: false exists for the service providers that cannot sign, Microsoft Entra ID federating its guests among them. A logout request is another matter: it is always signed, whatever the declaration says of the sign-on.

docs.title: The encryption it asks for
docs.text:
encrypt_assertions: true has every assertion of that service provider sent as a saml:EncryptedAssertion, never in clear. The declaration decides whether the assertions are encrypted; the metadata only decide which key they are encrypted for, which is the first certificate for encryption they list, read again when the response is written so that a key a refresh put in place meanwhile is the one used. A service provider that does not ask gets its assertions in clear, whatever keys its metadata hold.

What Value The content http://www.w3.org/2009/xmlenc11#aes256-gcm, a fresh key and IV for every assertion The key http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmlenc#rsa-oaep-mgf1p, whose mask is computed with SHA-1: it is what PHP wraps a key under and what SimpleSAMLphp unwraps, and the hash inside OAEP rests on no collision resistance The order The assertion is signed, then encrypted with its signature inside, then the response is signed over the ciphertext (SAML Core §6.2)

The md:EncryptionMethod elements of the metadata are not read, so no scheme is negotiated and none is downgraded: a service provider that cannot decrypt AES-GCM gets nothing it can read rather than an assertion in CBC. A request of a service provider that asks for encryption while its metadata hold no key for it is refused before anybody signs in, and nothing is sent in clear.

docs.title: Single logout
docs.text: A session of the provider can be ended from either side. A service provider asks for it with a LogoutRequest; or the session ends at the provider, and every service provider that signed in under it is told. Both go through the browser, the front channel of the Single Logout profile over HTTP-Redirect and HTTP-POST (SAML Profiles §4.4.3), at the single logout service of the tenant, /saml/slo.

docs.title: A logout a service provider asks for
docs.text:
The request is the service provider's, signed. A LogoutRequest is accepted from a declared service provider whose accepted metadata list a single logout service it can be answered at, and only signed, in its XML or over the query string of HTTP-Redirect, under the keys of its metadata (SAML Profiles §4.4.4.1). A declaration that says its sign-on requests are unsigned relaxes nothing here, and no setting does. A request that is refused ends nothing and gets no SAML answer: the browser is shown the page of a refusal.

Accepted once. The issuer and the ID of every request accepted are remembered until the window in which it would be accepted again has closed, eight minutes at most, in one store every worker of the deployment shares. The same request presented again ends nothing.

The sessions it names, of the person it names. A SessionIndex is the identifier of a session, the one the assertion carried, and a request names up to sixteen. A session is ended only when its user is the person of the NameID, a persistent identifier the provider computes again for that service provider and compares, never one it looks up.

The request The status of the answer Names sessions of that person, or sessions that have ended already, or that do not exist Success Names a session of another person Requester, UnknownPrincipal, and no session of the request ends Names no SessionIndex Requester, RequestUnsupported, and nothing ends

The sessions end as every session ends, at once and before the answer is written, since the answer says whether they ended (SAML Core §3.7.3.2). The clients of OpenID Connect that signed in under them are told by the back channel, their refresh tokens are revoked and their opaque access tokens removed, exactly as when the session ends at the end session endpoint. The other service providers of the session are told through the browser, in the chain below, before the one that asked is answered.

The answer goes where the metadata say. A signed LogoutResponse, to the first single logout service the accepted metadata list on the binding the request came over, or else the first one listed, at its ResponseLocation when it has one (SAML Metadata §2.2.2), never to an address the request carries. Its RelayState is the one received, byte for byte, and its status says PartialLogout under Success when one of the other service providers did not log out.

A key management service that does not answer when the signing key is opened ends nothing and answers 503: no session ends whose answer cannot be signed.

docs.title: The provider tells the others
docs.text:
The chain starts wherever a browser ends the session it holds:

  • the end session endpoint of OpenID Connect, once it has ended the session (RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 §2);
  • the sessions page of the account, when the session closed is the one of the browser reading it;
  • the single logout service, when a service provider's request ended sessions.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant P as Beffroi
    participant S1 as Service provider 1
    participant S2 as Service provider 2
    B->>P: Ends the session
    P->>B: The front-channel logout page of the OpenID Connect clients
    P->>B: LogoutRequest for service provider 1
    B->>S1: LogoutRequest
    S1->>B: LogoutResponse
    B->>P: LogoutResponse
    P->>B: LogoutRequest for service provider 2
    B->>S2: LogoutRequest
    S2->>B: LogoutResponse
    B->>P: LogoutResponse, then where the logout ends

The session has ended before the chain begins. Whatever becomes of the chain, a service provider that never answers or a browser closed half way, nothing of the provider stays open.

The OpenID Connect clients first. The browser is given the front-channel logout page of the ended sessions, one frame per client that registered a frontchannel_logout_uri (Front-Channel Logout 1.0 §2), and then goes on to the service providers.

Every service provider of the session, but the one that asked, session by session, in the order they first signed in. Each is sent a signed LogoutRequest: a new ID, valid five minutes, the persistent NameID computed again for it, one SessionIndex, and no RelayState, its answer being found by its InResponseTo. It goes to the first single logout service of its metadata, read again when it is written. Its LogoutResponse is read before the next one is told: signed, from that service provider, for that request. A status other than Success is an answer and not a refusal, and the chain goes on.

Passed over, and counted as a service provider that did not log out: one the configuration no longer declares, one whose metadata no longer read, one with no single logout service on HTTP-Redirect or HTTP-POST, one whose request cannot be written.

Kept by the provider, played once, by the browser that began it. Where the chain stands is a row of the provider and nothing the browser holds, since the session cookie no longer exists and an answer posted from another site arrives without it. The row is bound to the browser that began the chain by a cookie of its own, __Host-beffroi_saml_logout: Secure, HttpOnly, its path /, no Domain, SameSite=None because an answer over HTTP-POST is a post from another site, and worth the ten minutes the chain stays open, renewed at every step. A step presented without it, by the server of a service provider or by anybody who read a URL in a log, moves nothing.

Where it ends. For a logout a service provider asked for, its LogoutResponse. For the end session endpoint, the post_logout_redirect_uri with its state, as RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 §3 builds it, or the page that says the browser is signed out. For the page of the account, that page.

A service provider that never answers holds the browser where it is: the chain closes ten minutes after its last step, the service providers after it are not told, and the one that asked gets no answer. Nothing of the provider is held open by it.

docs.title: What a logout can promise
docs.text:
A session ended without its browser tells no service provider. The console, the page of the account read in another browser, closing every other session of an account, a new login that replaces a session: the clients of OpenID Connect learn it by the back channel, and a service provider has no channel without the browser, SOAP being out of scope.

Every end of a session revokes what was issued under it, whatever ended it: the refresh tokens of OpenID Connect issued in the session are revoked and its opaque access tokens removed.

The pages that start a chain name where it goes. The confirmation page of the end session endpoint and the sessions page of the account name, in their form-action, the origin of the single logout service each service provider of the session would be told at. A browser checks that directive over every redirection of a submission, and the chain is a series of them.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.text:
A service provider sends the browser to the single sign-on service of the tenant with an AuthnRequest, and the browser comes back to it with a signed Response. This is the Web Browser SSO profile (SAML Profiles §4.1), over the two bindings a browser can carry.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as Service provider
    participant P as Beffroi
    S->>B: AuthnRequest, to /saml/sso
    B->>P: GET (HTTP-Redirect) or POST (HTTP-POST)
    P->>B: The login page, unless a session answers
    B->>P: The person signs in
    P->>B: A page that posts the signed Response
    B->>S: POST to its assertion consumer service

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
The single sign-on service is /saml/sso, GET for HTTP-Redirect and POST for HTTP-POST, at the one URL the metadata publish. What is read, in this order:

  1. The binding. One message parameter, every parameter at most once under its own name, every input bounded before it is decoded. Over HTTP-Redirect, the signature is verified over the query string exactly as it arrived, SAMLRequest, RelayState and SigAlg in that order (SAML Bindings §3.4.4.1), never over a version rebuilt from the parsed parameters.
  2. The service provider. The one its Issuer names must be declared, and its metadata accepted.
  3. The signature. Required unless the service provider and its metadata both say it does not sign, and verified whenever it is there: the signature a request needs.
  4. The assertion consumer service. One of those the accepted metadata list. An AssertionConsumerServiceURL or an AssertionConsumerServiceIndex of the request is honoured only when it designates one of them, signed or not.

A request refused at any of these steps has nowhere trustworthy to be answered at, so it gets no SAML answer: the browser is shown a page that names the rule, and never a value of the message.

The RelayState is opaque. It is read up to 1024 bytes and given back byte for byte, where SAML Bindings §3.4.3 says 80: real service providers send longer ones, and the identity provider has to echo what it received.

A request posted from another site is posted again. Under SameSite=Lax a browser sends no session cookie with a POST coming from another site, which is exactly what the HTTP-POST binding is. A form posted from another site without the session cookie is answered with a page of the provider's own origin that posts the same body again, once, and the second post carries the session the browser holds: a person who is signed in is not asked to sign in again because the service provider chose that binding.

docs.title: What answers it
docs.text:
In this order, so that nobody signs in to be refused afterwards:

The request The answer A NameIDPolicy whose Format is neither persistent nor unspecified Requester, InvalidNameIDPolicy (SAML Core §3.4.1.1): the identity provider writes no other format A RequestedAuthnContext Responder, NoAuthnContext (SAML Core §3.3.2.2.1): the identity provider states no class of its own A browser holding an active session of the tenant, and, when the request says ForceAuthn="true", a proof made in the second the request arrived or later The assertion, at once IsPassive="true" and no session that answers Responder, NoPassive (SAML Core §3.4.1), without showing a page Anything else The login page of the provider

A failure is a Response of that status and no assertion, signed like every response and posted to the assertion consumer service of the metadata.

The login is the provider's, the page every flow signs in through, second factor and floor of the tenant included. The request waits for it in the session of the browser that sent it, never in a URL, under a reference drawn for it, for ten minutes, eight at most per browser, the oldest forgotten first. It is answered once and forgotten: a browser that comes back later, or that did not send it, finds nothing and is shown the page of a refusal.

One session for both protocols. The session is the one OpenID Connect opens. A person signed in by an OpenID Connect client reaches a service provider without signing in again, and the other way round.

docs.title: The response
docs.text:
What Value Signatures The assertion is signed, then the response over it, under RSA-SHA256, by the active SAML key of the tenant. Each signature carries in its KeyInfo the certificate the metadata publish for that key Issuer The entity ID of the tenant, the URL of its metadata, with no Format Destination, Recipient The assertion consumer service resolved from the metadata InResponseTo The ID of the request, on the response and on its bearer confirmation AudienceRestriction One Audience, the entity ID of the service provider Validity Five minutes: the Conditions run from the IssueInstant of the assertion, their NotBefore, to 300 seconds later, and the bearer confirmation ends with them AuthnStatement The AuthnInstant is the latest proof of the session; the SessionIndex is the identifier of the session, the one the sid of OpenID Connect carries; the class is urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:unspecified, and no SessionNotOnOrAfter Attributes The ones its declaration maps

The bearer confirmation carries no NotBefore, which SAML Profiles §4.1.4.2 forbids it. The KeyInfo is a hint for the service providers that need to tell which key signed, Microsoft Entra ID among them, and nothing more: whoever verifies the signature takes the key from the metadata, as Beffroi does.

docs.title: The NameID
docs.text:
The subject of the assertion is a persistent identifier (SAML Core §8.3.7), its NameQualifier the entity ID of the tenant and its SPNameQualifier the entity ID of the service provider. Its value is computed, never drawn and never stored:

base64url( SHA-256( entity ID of the service provider ‖ NUL ‖ sub ‖ NUL ‖ salt ‖ NUL ) )

Forty-three characters, without padding. The salt is the secret of the tenant its pairwise subjects are computed with (OIDC Core §8.1), sealed by the key management service. So:

  • the same person gets the same value at every login, in every worker, after a restore and after an import that keeps the subjects;
  • two service providers get two values they cannot relate to each other;
  • it is never the sub, nor a username nor an address, and nobody who knows the sub an OpenID Connect client holds can compute the NameID a service provider receives. SAML Core §8.3.7 asks for values with "no discernible correspondence with the subject's actual identifier".

docs.title: The page that posts it
docs.text:
The browser carries the response with a page that posts a form to the assertion consumer service: every name and value escaped for an HTML attribute, a one-line script that submits it and that its Content-Security-Policy allows by its hash and allows nothing else, default-src 'none', base-uri 'none' and frame-ancestors 'none', a button inside noscript for a browser without scripts, and Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store.

That page names no form-action. A browser checks that directive over every redirection a submission follows, and an assertion consumer service answers the post by sending the browser on to wherever its application lives, an origin no metadata state: Entra's login.srf, for one, sends it on to the client that asked Entra. A form-action there would leave the browser on a blank page. What it would still close, a form injected into the page, needs markup the page does not let in.

A success records that this service provider took part in the session, which is what single logout reads to tell it when the session ends.

docs.title: Upstream identity providers
docs.text: The tenant can sign a person in against the SAML identity provider of their organisation rather than with a credential of its own. For that it is a service provider, to the identity providers the deployment declares upstream of it, each one answering for the e-mail domains it names. This page is the role and its peers; signing in through an organisation is what a person goes through.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        service_provider:
            enabled: true
Option Default What it decides enabled false Whether the role exists. Off, nothing of it is wired, and its metadata, its assertion consumer service and its sign-on answer 404 entity_id the URL of its metadata The entity ID of the service provider, for one its identity providers already know by a name it keeps: an absolute URI of 1024 characters at most, with no whitespace, control, format or invisible character

The service provider signs with the SAML signing key of the identity provider, one key for both roles, rotated by the figures of beffroi.saml.identity_provider whichever role is on. A deployment that serves only this role draws that key the same way:

bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING

The two roles are two entities. The entity ID of the service provider is never the one of the identity provider of the tenant, which the configuration refuses whether that role is on or not, so turning it on later never makes the two one.

docs.title: Its metadata
docs.text:
Served at /saml/sp/metadata, which is also its entity ID unless entity_id names another. They hold:

  • one md:SPSSODescriptor of SAML 2.0, with AuthnRequestsSigned="true", since every request it sends is signed, and WantAssertionsSigned="true", so that an identity provider configured from them signs its assertion;
  • one KeyDescriptor use="signing" per SAML key in service, as the identity provider's metadata list them;
  • one assertion consumer service, on HTTP-POST, at /saml/sp/acs;
  • the cacheDuration of the identity provider's metadata, and no validUntil.

They list no single logout service, single logout with an upstream identity provider not being served, and no key for encryption: the certificate an identity provider encrypts for is published to that provider alone, below. Like the identity provider's, they are unsigned, and every URL in them comes from the configuration of the tenant.

docs.title: Declaring an identity provider
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    saml:
        service_provider: true
        identity_providers:
            'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata':
                metadata: 'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata'
                domains: ['example.org']
                email_attribute: mail
                profile:
                    givenName: given_name
                    sn: family_name
                groups:
                    attribute: memberOf
                    map:
                        staff: Staff
Option Default What it decides The key The entity ID of the identity provider, compared exactly with the one of its metadata. Never an entity ID of the tenant itself metadata required Where its metadata are read from: an https URL, no redirect followed, or the absolute path of a file of the deployment metadata_signers none The certificates its metadata are signed by, each the base64 of its DER. Named, the metadata are verified under them and must carry a validUntil domains required The e-mail domains it answers for, one at least and 256 at most email_attribute required The name of the attribute that carries the e-mail address of a person profile none The attributes that fill the profile of a person, keyed by the name of the attribute, each naming the claim it fills subject_attribute none The attribute that names a person when the NameID of an assertion is not persistent groups none The attribute that carries the groups of a person, and the group of the tenant each of its values stands for require_encrypted_assertions false An assertion arrives encrypted, or it is refused address_parameter none The parameter of its single sign-on service that takes the address the person typed, which it prefills its sign-in with

A declaration is refused while the service provider of the tenant is not enabled, and one that does not hold together fails the build of the deployment, the claims of profile included, which are checked right after the container is compiled. A declaration holding an environment variable is held to the same rules at its first use.

Domains. A domain is a name of the DNS, read without regard to case, a name outside ASCII written as its A-label. It is the whole part of an address after its @ and nothing under it: example.org does not answer for eu.example.org, which a provider that answers for it declares too. A domain answers to one identity provider of the tenant, and a domain two of them declare is refused, naming it and both providers: which provider answers for an address is never a choice.

The profile. One attribute per claim, among the claims a person can describe themselves with in this deployment: name, given_name, family_name, middle_name, nickname, preferred_username, birthdate, gender, locale, zoneinfo, profile, picture, website and phone_number, or whatever claims the deployment wires. email is not among them, since email_attribute carries it. A telephone number is written unverified: the provider filling it is not a proof that anybody verified it.

The subject. A person is named at their identity provider by a persistent NameID, a value it keeps for them. For an identity provider that sends another format, subject_attribute names the attribute that does the same job: a value that never changes, such as the object identifier Microsoft Entra ID sends, and never an address. The attribute of the e-mail is refused there, since an address is given again to somebody else, and the person hired under the address of one who left would be signed in to the account of that person.

Groups. Each value of the attribute is compared exactly with the keys of map, 256 values at most, and a value the map does not name is no group. The groups the map names are groups of the tenant, found by their name, and none is ever created from what an identity provider sends: create them first.

bin/console beffroi:group:create Staff

docs.title: Its metadata, read and kept
docs.text:
Exactly as a service provider's are, by the same objects: read from the declared location, verified under pinned signers or trusted by their channel, refused when expired, never older than the document accepted when they are signed, sealed where they sit, and refreshed every hour by the timed step. They are refused besides when they hold no md:IDPSSODescriptor of SAML 2.0, no key for signing, or a single sign-on service that is not https on a host.

bin/console beffroi:saml:identity-provider:refresh
bin/console beffroi:saml:identity-provider:forget 'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata'

An identity provider whose metadata were never accepted cannot be signed in through: read them before announcing the domain to anybody.

docs.title: The key it encrypts for
docs.text:
An identity provider that encrypts its assertions encrypts them for a key of the tenant, and each identity provider has one of its own, never shared with another nor with the signing key. Its algorithm names the provider:

bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm='SAML-ENCRYPTION:https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata'

It is an RSA key of the tenant like the others, sealed by the key management service, absent from the JWK Set so that no OpenID Connect client encrypts to it, and rotated with the commands and the timed step of every key, by the figures of the SAML signing key: seven days staged, a year of work.

Its certificate goes to that provider alone. The metadata of the service provider for one identity provider are served at /saml/sp/metadata/ followed by the entity ID of that provider in base64url, without padding (RFC 4648 §5):

printf '%s' 'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata' | basenc --base64url --wrap=0 | tr -d '='

They are the metadata above, with one KeyDescriptor use="encryption" per key of that provider staged or active, the newest first, and none of another provider. An identity provider takes the first certificate it finds, so listing the staged key first is what makes it encrypt for the next key days before that key takes over; the retiring key is no longer announced, and still opens what was encrypted for it until it retires. The certificate is self-signed, its one extension keyUsage with keyEncipherment alone. The URL answers 404 while the tenant holds no key in service for that provider.

A ciphertext of a provider is opened by the keys of that provider, and by no other. The keys tried are those of the identity provider whose metadata verified the response, its staged, active and retiring ones in turn; the KeyInfo of the encrypted key is not read. A key shared between two providers would let one of them carry the other's ciphertext under its own signature and read what the decryption answers, which is why there is one key per provider.

What arrives What happens AES-GCM, its key under RSA-OAEP Decrypted AES-CBC, in a response whose own signature verifies Decrypted, the signature covering the ciphertext. Entra, AD FS and SimpleSAMLphp encrypt under CBC AES-CBC, in a response that is not signed Refused by name: CBC authenticates nothing, so it is opened only under a signature An encrypted assertion from a provider the tenant holds no key for Refused by name An assertion in clear from a provider declared with require_encrypted_assertions: true Refused before anything of it is read

Every cryptographic failure of a decryption is one and the same refusal, so that nothing in the answer tells a padding from a key.

docs.title: SCIM
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

No SCIM endpoint is served at this point. This page says what is decided, so that nobody has to guess from an empty section. It will be replaced by the documentation of the endpoints the day they exist.

SCIM is how a directory pushes its people into a provider instead of being asked for them: Entra ID and Okta both speak it, and for a company already running one, provisioning through SCIM is what makes an identity provider usable without anyone creating a single user by hand.

docs.title: What it will serve
docs.text: The receiving half, first: /Users and /Groups as RFC 7644 defines them, over the schema of RFC 7643. Beffroi is the target of the provisioning, which is what Entra and Okta know how to drive, and what their own validators judge.

docs.title: What is already decided
docs.text:
• Groups carry a source. The identity model holds, for every membership, where it came from: written in this provider, asserted by an upstream identity provider, or pushed by a directory. A directory may not quietly take over a group somebody created here, and what it pushed must be distinguishable from what was written by hand. That is a property of the groups model, and it exists before SCIM does.
  • The provenance model is the one federation uses. What SCIM pushes and what a federated sign-in brings back are the same question asked twice: who told us this, and may they change it. A person already names the source that created them, and what a source holds a manual description does not change: a directory will be one more source, under the same rule.
  • The connector is judged from outside. The success criterion is the Entra and Okta connectors, and their validators, against this provider. Not a test suite of our own.

docs.title: What it will not do
docs.text: Beffroi will not push to other directories, and will not be a SCIM client. Signing a person in against the identity provider of their organisation is federation, not provisioning, and it has its own place in the SAML section.
