docs.text: title: The Symfony bundle description: What beffroi/symfony-bundle adds to an application: configuration, routes, persistence, security, pages and commands.

docs.title: The Symfony bundle
docs.text: beffroi/symfony-bundle is the only place in Beffroi where Symfony appears. A Request, the container, the entity manager, a Twig template and a console command live here and nowhere else, which is what keeps the packages underneath usable without a framework.

docs.title: What it brings
docs.text: Page What it covers Configuration One tree under beffroi, section by section, validated when the container is built Routes and planes The controllers of both planes, and BEFFROI_PLANE to restrict a process to one Persistence The Doctrine mapping, the migrations, and the DBAL types that read value objects back Security The firewalls, the authenticators, and what a session carries Key management The key management client the private keys are sealed with Pages Login, consent, logout, device, and how to make them yours Translations Every user-facing string, in XLIFF, and how a page decides which language it speaks Messenger Which writes are asynchronous, and which ones the protocol waits for The account pages What a person sees of themselves, and what they can take back Console commands Tenant, users, groups, clients, keys, data keys, SAML metadata, FIDO metadata The profiler panel What the provider did during a request, in the Symfony profiler

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text:
composer require beffroi/symfony-bundle

Installation, in full

docs.title: Conventions it follows
docs.text:
Knowing these makes the rest of this section predictable.

  • A controller is final readonly, one action per class, with the route on __invoke(). There is no controller with six methods.
  • A route name carries its plane: beffroi_protocol_* is server to server, beffroi_interaction_* is a browser. Nothing is ambiguous, and a process can be restricted to one of the two.
  • A value object a column holds whole goes in one column, with a DBAL type of the bundle that reads it back through the object's own constructor, rather than a Doctrine embeddable fixing one type per field for the whole model. One embeddable is left in the mapping, embedded by one entity, and it is named where the mapping is described.
  • No write is synchronous unless the protocol needs its result in the same request. Every exception is listed in the Messenger configuration with the reason it is one.
  • Every user-facing string is translated. A signed-in person reads the pages in the language of their record; for anybody else the language comes from what the browser asked for, then ui_locales, then Accept-Language, and never from the URL.
  • A test never sleeps. Time moves with a mocked clock, which survives a kernel reboot.

docs.title: The account pages
docs.text:
A person signs in at the issuer, reads what the provider holds of them, and takes any of it back without asking an administrator. The same facts are available to an operator through the console, and the two read the same code.

None of these pages belongs to a client or to an authorization request. They are reached by typing the issuer in a browser, and the home of the account is where they hang from: every other page carries the link back to it, and nothing else.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
The home is a card per page, in this order, each card carrying what the account holds there. The titles below are the ones the English catalogue carries.

Page Path What is on it Requests waiting for you /account/approvals What somebody is waiting on an answer for right now. It is first because every other card says what the account holds and this one says that a request is open Your information /account/profile What the provider holds of this person: the name they sign in with, the two dates of the record, and one line per claim of OIDC Core §5.1 Your passkeys /account/passkeys Their passkeys, with the name each one was given, its dates and its state Two-factor authentication /account/two-factor The authenticator application, when there is one, and how many backup codes are left Applications you have allowed /account/consents One line per client in force, with the scopes it holds, and a page per application behind it Where you are signed in /account/sessions Where this person is signed in at this moment, what each session proved, and where it was last seen Your password /account/password When the password was last written, and the form that replaces it What happened to your account /account/acts What the journal holds of the account: who signed in as them and with what, the attempts that were refused, what signed out, what changed of the means of signing in and what they did of their own record. Its card counts the refused attempts the journal holds, twenty at most, since a failure is what somebody comes to look for Notifications /account/notifications The browsers this provider can reach by web push Your data /account/archive The one file holding everything the provider knows of them, and where their last request for it has got to

The subject identifier clients know this person by is on none of them. It is the sub of a token, not something a person comes to read of themselves, and a client of a sector that asked for a pairwise identifier is given a different one, so a page naming one of them would be saying something false.

Every route, with the one each form posts to

docs.title: What a person may change of themselves
docs.text:
The information page is one line per claim this provider can hold, read where it is held and written where the tenant opens it: the same thing is not read in one list and offered in another, so the line somebody corrects is the line they were reading. What the tenant opens is tenant.self_served_claims, a rule of the tenant and never an option of the deployment, and a tenant that opens none of them serves a page that only reads.

A claim says what field it is, which is what the page renders: the kind its input carries, the whole set when the set is closed, and the pattern or the length when it is not. A closed set is closed on the server too, for every caller and not only for that page, and a birthdate that is not a date is refused rather than stored. What those lines said before, and when they changed, is at /account/profile/changes.

docs.title: What the password page says
docs.text:
Besides the date the password was last written and the form that replaces it, the password page is where a person is told something rather than asked: a password already in use that a list of compromised values was later found to hold. The lookup happens after a login, on a lane, at most once a month per person, so no sign-in waits on somebody else's service, and the answer outlives the request that noticed it.

So the person is not left to find it: the next login that serves no authorization request sends them to this page, which says why, before the page they were going to, and asks again at every such login until the password is replaced. A login that answers an authorization request of OpenID Connect is not diverted; the logins a page of the provider asks for are, the pages of the account, the approval of a device or of a backchannel request, and the single sign-on of a SAML service provider among them.

A password posed here is typed twice and the two are compared in constant time, and the counter beside the field is local to the browser: what the page says of a password as it is typed asks nobody anything, and a password is never sent anywhere to be scored. The length it asks for is the one the floor of the tenant sets, fifteen characters or eight, and the field and the core read the same number.

Passwords

docs.title: A person of an organisation
docs.text: A person whose address is of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for signs in at their organisation and nowhere else. The pages of their account offer no form that would pose a password, a passkey or an authenticator application, and say so: their organisation signs them in, no password, passkey or authenticator application of this account signs them in, and none is added to it. A form posted by hand is refused all the same, and what the source of their account holds of their profile is read there and not changed.

docs.title: What a page asks before it opens
docs.text:
A page of the account needs the session this browser holds, and the form token when it posts. Without the session it refuses with login_required, and the refusal offers the home of the account, which is the one page of the plane that sends a browser to the login and brings it back: there is nowhere else to send it, a page of the account belonging to no client and to no interaction.

A session outlives the moment it was opened, by construction: a person signs in once and reads their account for the rest of the day, and so does whoever sits down in front of a screen left unlocked. That is the right trade for a page that shows what the account holds, and the wrong one for the gesture somebody else would lock its owner out with, so a page that adds or takes away a way in asks for the proof again when the session was opened more than five minutes ago.

Asks for a recent proofReached on the session alone

The password page and the form that replaces it, the passkeys page, the enrolment of a passkey and its revocation, the second factor page, its enrolment, its revocation and the renewal of its backup codes.

The proof is asked for by the login of the firewall, the one every other page of the provider uses, so what this person holds is what proves them again: a password, a passkey or a code. Nothing here asks for a kind, which would be a page deciding what a credential is worth in place of the tenant's policy.

Everything that reads, plus ending a session, closing every other session, renaming a passkey and the options of a ceremony.

Ending a session is not taking away a way in: a session is closed because it is feared, and asking for a password first would be asking somebody to type it on the browser they are worried about. It is the one gesture of these pages that can only ever put an attacker outside.

Which pages ask is declared by the pages themselves, and the rule is applied before the controller runs, so it bounds the GET and the POST of a page alike: a guard a form does not repeat is a guard that a form submission walks around.

docs.title: Enrolling a second factor
docs.text:
The enrolment is the two steps it is, handing the secret to an authenticator application and then confirming the code that application shows. The provisioning URI is drawn as an SVG QR code by the bundle itself and embedded in the page, with no image loaded from anywhere: that URI carries the secret, and a QR code service would read it. The same key is printed in base32 in groups of four for a person who types it, and taken in one click.

What was drawn lives in the session of that browser for ten minutes, sealed by the key management service of the tenant, and nowhere else: an enrolment abandoned in front of the QR code leaves nothing behind. A code that does not match renders the same page with the same QR code, so the application is not rescanned.

The ten backup codes are shown exactly once, as the response to the request that confirmed the enrolment: one numbered block taken in one click, hashed in the row, and displayed by nothing afterwards. Drawing another set replaces the previous one whole.

docs.title: Every table reads the same way
docs.text:
What a reader learns of one table serves them on the others.

  • Paging is one word in the query string, page, and one number of rows, twenty, for all of them. The control under a table is rendered only where there is more than one page, a page nobody can reach is the same words without a link, and a number past the last page is the last page.
  • A period is two words, from and to, read on the clock of the person the page is served to. Each table reads the date a reader looks for: an act by when it happened, a session by when it was opened, a passkey or a browser by when it was enrolled, a consent by when it was given.
  • An empty table keeps its head and says which of the two emptinesses it is, nothing at all or nothing over those days, rather than replacing itself with a sentence.
  • Where a request came from reads the same way everywhere: the place the enrichment of a provenance derived from the address, and the browser the user agent names. A deployment that derives no place says the address and no place.

docs.title: Taking it back
docs.text: On this page The gesture What it does Applications you have allowed Revoke Takes back the consent and the access that client holds. The next authorization request asks again Where you are signed in Close Ends that session and revokes the tokens issued under it; its OpenID Connect clients are told through the back channel, and when it is the session of this very browser, its SAML service providers are told through it before the page comes back Where you are signed in Close every other one Ends every session of this person but the one reading the page, with the same revocation and the same back channel. Those sessions have no browser here, so their SAML service providers are not told Your passkeys Revoke Revokes that credential. The line stays, listed as revoked Two-factor authentication Remove Revokes the authenticator. The sessions it completed stay as they are Notifications Revoke Drops that subscription, and this provider stops reaching that browser

docs.title: Your data
docs.text:
A person asks for everything the provider holds of them and is handed one file, structured and machine readable, which is what GDPR article 20 asks for. The page says where the last request has got to: never asked, being built, ready, stalled, or expired.

  • It expires a week after it was asked for, and that week is a figure in the code rather than an option: every day that file exists is a day it exists. The expiry is counted from the ask and not from the build, so a request that never ran is forgotten on the same day as one that did.
  • A build is given a quarter of an hour. Past that, the page says nobody is building this one rather than showing a week of work in progress, and asking again opens a new request in its place.
  • It leaves under a passphrase when the person wants one. The file is then wrapped, and the floor on the length of that passphrase, sixteen characters, is refused rather than warned about: what stands between that file and whoever took it is the length of what was typed. A person who asks for no passphrase downloads the file as it was built.
  • It is sealed where it sits like every other personal column, in a scope of its own. It is the one file in which everything this provider knows of a person stands in clear at once, so it carries no exemption.
  • It is dropped when they say so, in whatever state the request is in: a file they already downloaded is a file this provider no longer holds, and a build still on its way finds nothing to write to, which is what makes a request something a person can take back. The row goes rather than staying as a row marked dropped, since the only state worth keeping of that file is none.

What is in it is one chapter per family the provider holds: the profile, the credentials, the linked identities, the groups, what was consented to, the sessions, the journal of the acts, and what the record used to say.

Personal data

docs.title: What a form answers
docs.text:
Every form of these pages answers 303 See Other towards the page it came from, accepted or refused, so reloading reads the page again instead of sending the form a second time. A refusal travels in the session of that browser for the one reading that follows: a code the page translates and the field it is about, never the value that was typed.

Three answers are the response itself and are read once: the backup codes that end an enrolment, the notice that the session this browser was reading on has ended, and an archive wrapped under a passphrase, which is the file.

docs.title: Dates and language
docs.text:
A signed-in person reads these pages in the language of their record, and changes it where that record is changed. A date is written on the clock that person holds, with the words and the order of the language the page is written in, and the clock is always named: an hour without its zone is an hour a reader cannot check.

Translations

docs.title: Adding a page
docs.text: A page of the account is a class implementing Beffroi\Bundle\Http\Account\AccountSectionInterface, tagged beffroi.account_section: it names the route it opens, the key of its title and what this account holds there. The home reads the tagged sections in the order they are wired, so a page added is a class and a line in the wiring, and neither the home nor its template is edited. Two sections naming one route are a fault of the wiring, and they are refused as such.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The configuration is one tree, built from a class per section, validated when the container is built rather than when a request arrives. A section a deployment leaves out is a feature it does not serve: a tenant with no client_registration has no registration endpoint, in its discovery document as on the wire.

This page will describe each section and what it decides. The exhaustive tree is in the reference.

docs.title: Console commands
docs.text:
The bundle adds the commands for the tenant, users and their journal, groups, clients, keys, data keys, SAML metadata, the databases of addresses and FIDO metadata. They are listed, grouped and described in the reference.

This page will describe the ones that need explaining beyond their help: the rotation of a key, the rewrapping of data keys, and the destruction that cannot be undone.

docs.title: Installing the bundle
docs.text:
Three things happen at installation: the bundle is registered, its routes are imported under the path of the issuer, and its Doctrine migrations are run. Getting started walks through all three.

This page will describe the installation in detail, including what Flex does for you, what a deployment that serves two planes imports, and how to check the result.

docs.title: Key management
docs.text:
The bundle seals private keys with a client of symfony/key-management, named in the configuration and declared where that component is configured. Which provider it talks to, and whether there are several, is a decision of the deployment and not of the bundle.

This page will describe the clients available, what each one needs, and how to move from one to another.

docs.title: Messenger
docs.text:
No write is synchronous unless the protocol needs its result in the same request, and every exception is listed in the Messenger configuration with the reason it is one. Messages are commands, queries, events or explicitly synchronous messages, and a handler calls a use case rather than holding logic of its own.

The buses, their middleware and where each kind of message is sent are a contract the bundle prepends to the Messenger configuration of the application, not a preference of whoever installs it: an installation that wires them itself and turns the default middleware off, or gets the Doctrine transaction middleware wrong, breaks the asynchronous half of the provider quietly. What is left to an application is its transports, and the lanes fall back to the database, so a new installation needs no broker to work.

The body of every message leaves the process sealed. What a column seals, a queue may not carry in clear: a message is sealed as a JWE towards the encryption key of the tenant, so what a broker, the table of a transport or the failure transport holds is worth nothing without the key management service. The sender holds the public half only and asks the key management service for nothing; the consumer unseals the private half once per process. That key is a key of the tenant like the others, rotated and rewrapped like them, and it is never published in the JWK Set: a key at the JWK Set is a key any reader of the discovery document could seal a body under.

The transport headers carry the tenant, so a consumer knows which key to ask for before it touches the body and a failed message can be read without being opened. What decides is the protected header of the JWE, which is the authenticated data: a header swapped in transit makes the unsealing fail rather than succeed under another scope.

What time does on its own is one recurring message per step, handled on the command bus like every other write, so a deployment that runs the worker runs them.

This page will describe the transports, the queues, what runs where, and what happens when the broker is down.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
The bundle ships the pages a person sees, styled with Tailwind, translated, and overridable like any Twig template of any bundle. They are deliberately plain: a provider's pages are the deployment's own, not the project's advertisement.

What a tenant shows of itself is on every page: its name, the logo it names, and the two colours it names, the one the buttons and the links are drawn in and the colour of what is written on them. They are read from the tenant at every render rather than hard-coded in a template, so a deployment that declares none of them is served the pages it has always been served. The logo is loaded by the browser of the visitor and never by the provider, and the pages name its origin in their content policy.

The login page offers what the tenant admits. It shows the logins the firewall wires that the floor of the tenant accepts: a tenant that signs its people in by passkey shows no password field and no username, the passkey naming its own user. A tenant that federates domains to upstream identity providers asks for the address first, one field and nothing else, and sends an address of those domains to its provider.

Three pages post a form for the browser. One answers a client that asked for response_mode=form_post (OAuth 2.0 Form Post Response Mode); one carries a SAML message to a peer, a response or a logout message to a service provider, a request to an upstream identity provider; the third posts again, from the provider's own origin, a form another site posted without the session cookie. Each submits itself with the one script its content policy allows by its hash, and keeps a button for a browser that runs no script. Their words are translated like every other page's.

This page will describe each page, the blocks to override, and what must not be removed from them.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
The model is mapped with XML, outside the entities, and a value object a column holds whole goes in one column with a DBAL type of the bundle that reads it back through the object's own constructor. An embeddable would fix the type of each of its fields once for the whole model, so the same kind of value could not be sealed in one table and readable in another, which is why there is one embeddable in the mapping and not a family of them: the authorization request, embedded by one entity, whose first field is an entity no mapping carries.

This page will describe the schema, the migrations, the types, and what a sealed column changes about a query.

docs.title: The profiler panel
docs.text:
In development the bundle adds a panel to the Symfony profiler: the client, the grant, what was checked, what was issued, and what the key management service was asked. It is off wherever the profiler is off, and it is never what a measurement is read from.

This page will describe what the panel shows.

docs.title: Routes and planes
docs.text:
Every route of the bundle carries its plane in its name: beffroi_protocol_* for what a client or a resource server calls, beffroi_interaction_* for what a browser reads. BEFFROI_PLANE restricts a process to one of them, so a provider can serve the protocol on machines a browser never reaches.

This page will describe the import, the planes, and what a request to the wrong plane gets. The endpoints lists every route.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The bundle brings its own authenticators for the interaction plane and expects nothing of the host application's security configuration beyond a firewall to put them on. The provider's session is its own: it records what was proven, and it is not the host application's login session.

Besides the one of its development tools, the standalone application declares two firewalls: the protocol endpoints, which authenticate their clients themselves and open no session, and the interaction pages, where the logins of the provider live.

config/packages/security.yaml
security:
    providers:
        beffroi:
            id: Beffroi\Bundle\Security\IdentityUserProvider
    firewalls:
        beffroi_protocol:
            pattern: ^/(\.well-known/(openid-configuration|oauth-authorization-server)|jwks|token|userinfo|introspect|revoke|par|device_authorization|backchannel_authentication|register(/.+)?)$
            security: false
        beffroi_interaction:
            lazy: true
            provider: beffroi
            user_checker: Beffroi\Bundle\Security\UserChecker
            entry_point: Beffroi\Bundle\Security\PasswordLoginAuthenticator
            custom_authenticators:
                - Beffroi\Bundle\Security\PasswordLoginAuthenticator
                - Beffroi\Bundle\Security\PasskeyLoginAuthenticator
                - Beffroi\Bundle\Security\TotpLoginAuthenticator
                - Beffroi\Bundle\Security\UpstreamAssertionAuthenticator

Each authenticator is one way in: a password, a passkey, the code of a second factor, and the assertion an upstream SAML identity provider posts to the assertion consumer service. Every one of them ends in the same place: the core opens the session under the floor of the tenant, or records the new proofs on the session the browser already holds for that person, so the order of a login is written once whichever door it came through.

A post from another site sets no session cookie. Under SameSite=Lax a browser keeps the session cookie back from a POST that comes from another site. A page of the interaction plane answering such a post with the cookie of a new session would replace the one the browser holds and sign it out of the provider, so that cookie is taken off the answer. The five endpoints another site posts a browser to on purpose, the authorization endpoint, the end session endpoint, the SAML single sign-on and single logout services and the assertion consumer service, post the request again from the provider's own origin instead, and the second post carries the session. Both read where the post comes from in Sec-Fetch-Site (Fetch Metadata Request Headers): a browser that does not send it is answered as it always was.

This page will describe the authenticators in full, and the rate limits that apply.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text:
Every user-facing string goes through the translator, in XLIFF with intl-icu for plurals and parameters, in the beffroi domain. The bundle ships en and fr:

translations/beffroi+intl-icu.en.xlf
translations/beffroi+intl-icu.fr.xlf

An application replaces a sentence by putting the same key in its own translations/beffroi+intl-icu.fr.xlf, which Symfony loads after the catalogues of the bundles. Adding a language is one more catalogue of the same domain, and framework.enabled_locales naming it.

The error_description of the protocol is not translated

It is addressed to the developer of the client, in ASCII, as RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 asks. What a person reads on the error page is the translated sentence of the error code, and the description sits under it, in the language of the specification.

docs.title: Two lists of languages, two questions
docs.text:
List What it answers Where it comes from The languages this deployment serves What a page can be written in framework.enabled_locales, with framework.default_locale in front The languages a person can say they read What the locale claim of a person may name Every locale ICU has data for, each under its own name in itself

They are two lists because they answer two questions: locale is a claim of OIDC Core §5.1 and not a setting of this provider, so a provider whose pages speak two languages still holds the claim of somebody who reads a third. What that claim names is read against the first list wherever it is the language of a page or of a message.

A tag is matched as Symfony matches an Accept-Language: fr-CA gives fr_CA when that locale is served and fr otherwise, a script subtag is kept, and a tag no served locale matches is ignored rather than refused.

docs.title: Which language a page speaks
docs.text:
A signed-in person reads the pages in the language of their record, and changes it where that record is changed. That is the first answer tried, before anything the browser asked for. A record that names nothing, or names a language this deployment does not serve, leaves the rest of the chain untouched.

For a visitor who is not known yet, the language of an interaction is chosen once, on arrival at /authorize, and kept on the interaction so the next page of the same journey reads in it:

  1. the language this browser asked for;
  2. ui_locales of the request, read against the served languages;
  3. Accept-Language, read the same way;
  4. the default locale of the deployment.

What the visitor asked for comes before ui_locales because ui_locales is an end-user preference the client passes on (OIDC Core §3.1.2.1), which is a second hand, and somebody who has just named their language on the page is the first. Pages with no interaction behind them, an error before the first step of an authorization, an unknown page, the logout confirmation and the page after it, speak the language of the browser; the logout reads the ui_locales of its own request first, as RP-Initiated Logout §2 allows.

The language is never in the URL. The relying party does not know it, and a login URL that changes with the language is a second address for every page.

docs.title: How a person chooses one
docs.text:
A form and no script: POST /locale, one button per language the deployment serves, rendered wherever the layout of the application includes the switcher. Below two languages there is nothing to offer and the control is not rendered at all, and a page whose language was decided by the record of a signed-in person says so, so the control offers nothing there either.

What is asked for is read against the served languages, and a tag nobody serves changes nothing. The choice is then written in three places, because they answer three questions:

Where What it answers The locale slot of the preferences of this browser The language the next journey from this browser starts in The interaction in progress The language its next page is read in The locale claim of the account, when somebody is signed in The language this provider writes to that person in, outside any request of theirs

The claim is written on a lane, nothing in the request waiting on the result, and it replaces that claim and nothing else: describing a whole profile is what provisioning does, and it clears what it is not told.

The preferences of a browser travel on one cookie, __Host-beffroi_preferences, with a slot per preference: the language this visitor asked for, the theme they read the pages in, and whatever a preference wired beside them declares. It is read by no script, never leaves the requests of that browser, goes out over TLS only and is worth a year, so somebody who said it once is not asked again. It is not the HTTP session, deliberately: the protocol plane opens no session, a language in one would open a session for every visitor who never signed in, and signing out invalidates a session whole, which would lose a choice made for a year.

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
A date a person reads says which clock it is on, and neither of the two things that decide it belongs to the provider.

  • The clock is the one that person holds. zoneinfo is a claim of OIDC Core §5.1, so it is read as a zone rather than taken for one: it may be absent, and it may name a zone this process cannot resolve, in which case the clock of the deployment answers.
  • The words and the order are ICU's, in the language the page is written in. A date is not a string to translate but a convention of a locale, so a deployment that serves a language gets the dates of that language without writing a catalogue entry for them.

The zone is always named, by its abbreviation when it has one and by its offset otherwise: an hour without its zone is an hour a reader cannot check. The machine readable form stays in the datetime attribute of the element that carries it, which gives the instant with its offset. The dates the console prints do not go through any of this, an administrator reading them beside a server.

The bundle requires ext-intl, which its own +intl-icu catalogues already needed.

docs.title: Web push
docs.text:
A deployment that names a push subject lets the tenant draw an application server key and reach a person through the push service of a browser they signed in with, which is how a decoupled request can be confirmed without a second application. Nothing in a notification names the request it is about.

This page will describe the subscription, the encryption, what a notification carries, and what a 410 from a push service does.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text: Loyalty is to the standard, not to a reading of the standard, so the protocol is judged from outside. The conformance suite of the OpenID Foundation is open source, free to run, and it runs against the provider in continuous integration.

docs.title: The plans that run
docs.text:
Each plan is a certification plan of the suite, played in --strict, the mode a certification submission asks for: a warning there is a failure. Only the results a human must read on the plan's page, and the ones the suite itself decides to skip, stay acceptable, because no run can avoid them.

Family Plans OpenID Connect Core Basic OP, Config OP, Form Post Basic OP Logout RP-Initiated Logout OP, Front-Channel Logout OP, Back-Channel Logout OP FAPI 2.0 Security DPoP, Security mTLS, Signing DPoP, Signing mTLS FAPI-CIBA Poll, Ping Registration and bootstrap Dynamic OP, Third Party-Init OP, Rotate Keys

A module that stays red is listed with its reason and the issue that closes it, and the run then fails the day it starts passing, so the line gets deleted rather than carried. The current state of every plan lives in the code repository, beside the workflow that runs them, because that is where it is maintained.

docs.title: SAML 2.0
docs.text:
There is no certification programme for SAML 2.0, so the judges are the implementations the provider has to work with, and tools that are not its own. Nothing the provider says of a signature it wrote counts as a proof of that signature.

Judge What it plays When xmlsec1 and the OpenSSL command line Every signature and every ciphertext the SAML packages write, under every algorithm the build supports, verified and decrypted; every signed HTTP-Redirect URL verified over the octets of the binding In continuous integration, at every pull request SimpleSAMLphp A service provider of the identity provider, over both bindings, with an encrypted assertion and single logout started from either side; the upstream identity provider of the service provider, with a first sign-in, its groups and an encrypted assertion By hand, against a running provider Microsoft Entra ID Federating its guests to the identity provider; the upstream identity provider of a tenant through an enterprise application By hand, against a Microsoft tenant Keycloak The messages of the model and the bindings, both ways By hand

Besides those judges, the published corpora of attacks on XML signatures are part of the suites of the packages, and every invariant of their specifications has its tests.

docs.title: What the mark means, and what it does not
docs.text:
Beffroi is not OpenID Certified yet

Running the suite and being certified are two different things. The runs above are free and reproducible; the mark is a filing with the OpenID Foundation for a given deployment and a given major version. It will be announced here, with the entry in the public list, the day it is filed.

Certification qualifies the software. It says nothing about the organisation that operates a deployment, which is what ISO 27001 and the national cloud qualifications are for. Those apply to a hosted service, never to a bundle you install yourself.

docs.title: Running the suite yourself
docs.text: The suite is a set of Docker images you can run locally against your own deployment, with no account and no limit on the number of runs. The plans the project uses, and the task that drives them through the suite's API, are in the code repository.

docs.title: Reporting something
docs.text: What Where A bug, a question about the protocol, a missing feature beffroi-auth/beffroi A page of this site that is wrong, unclear or missing beffroi-auth/docs A vulnerability Privately, through the security advisories of the code repository. Never in a public issue

docs.title: Sending a patch to the code
docs.text:
One issue, one branch, one pull request. The branch is named type/<issue>-<slug>, for instance feat/162-dpop, and the commit message says what the change does: type(scope): what it does, lowercase, no final period (issue #N).

Target the branch of the version your change belongs to: a fix goes to the oldest branch it applies to, a feature to the newest. The quality gate runs on every pull request: the test suite, static analysis at the maximum level, the architecture rules, the formatter, and mutation testing on the lines you changed.

Tests have a fixed shape in this project. One test verifies one behaviour, laid out in // Given, // When and // Then blocks, and its name cites the section of the specification it verifies.

docs.title: Editing a page of this site
docs.text:
Every page has a pencil at the top right that opens it in GitHub, on the branch of the version you are reading. For more than a typo, clone the repository and run the site locally:

git clone git@github.com:beffroi-auth/docs.git
cd docs
make install
make serve

The site is then on http://127.0.0.1:8000, rebuilt as you save. Before opening the pull request:

make check

That is the same build continuous integration runs: a strict build, where a broken internal link, a missing anchor or a page absent from the navigation is an error.

docs.title: The rules a page follows
docs.text:
• A page states the present state. It never tells how it got there, and it carries no changelog of its own.
  • One page, one subject, named in its title. The navigation is the table of contents.
  • A page that is not written yet carries status: draft in its front matter, and the navigation shows a pencil. Better an honest stub than a page that sounds finished.
  • Specifications are cited by number and section, for instance RFC 9449 §4.3 or OIDC Core §3.1.3.7.
  • English, full sentences, no dashes used as punctuation.
  • A figure, a limit or a default that appears on a page must be the one the code applies.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Beffroi is developed as one monorepo, beffroi-auth/beffroi, and published as eight packages. Each package is split read-only into its own repository, so you can read the history of one part without the rest.

Package Namespace What it is Repository beffroi/core Beffroi\Core The identity model: tenants, people, credentials, linked identities, groups, sessions, keys beffroi-auth/core beffroi/oidc Beffroi\Oidc OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect beffroi-auth/oidc beffroi/saml Beffroi\Saml SAML 2.0, the identity provider and the service provider of a tenant beffroi-auth/saml beffroi/saml2-model Beffroi\Saml2\Model The SAML 2.0 messages, assertions and metadata, read strictly and written beffroi-auth/saml2-model beffroi/saml2-bindings Beffroi\Saml2\Bindings The HTTP-Redirect and HTTP-POST bindings beffroi-auth/saml2-bindings beffroi/xml-security Beffroi\Xml A safe DOM, XML Signature and XML Encryption beffroi-auth/xml-security beffroi/symfony-bundle Beffroi\Bundle The Symfony integration beffroi-auth/symfony-bundle beffroi/op App The standalone application beffroi-auth/op

docs.title: Which one do I install?
docs.text:
I run a Symfony applicationI want a provider of its ownI am not using SymfonyI only need to read and write SAML

Require beffroi/symfony-bundle. It pulls the core and both protocols with it, and brings the controllers, the Doctrine mapping, the console commands and the login and consent pages.

Installing the bundle

Deploy beffroi/op, the standalone application. It is the bundle, a Symfony skeleton, FrankenPHP and nothing you have to assemble yourself.

The standalone application

Require beffroi/oidc, beffroi/saml, or both. They are pure PHP: they know no HTTP, no container and no ORM, and they talk to the world through ports you implement.

The ports of the protocol

Require beffroi/saml2-bindings, which brings beffroi/saml2-model and beffroi/xml-security. They know nothing of Beffroi: the messages, their signatures and their encryption, for any PHP project that speaks SAML.

The SAML packages

docs.title: What depends on what
docs.text:
The direction never reverses. The core knows nothing of the protocols, the protocols know nothing of each other nor of Symfony, and the bundle is the only place where a Request, a container or a Doctrine entity manager appears.

graph RL
  op["beffroi/op<br/><small>the application</small>"] --> bundle["beffroi/symfony-bundle"]
  bundle --> oidc["beffroi/oidc"]
  bundle --> saml["beffroi/saml"]
  bundle --> core["beffroi/core"]
  oidc --> core
  saml --> core
  saml --> bindings["beffroi/saml2-bindings"]
  bindings --> model["beffroi/saml2-model"]
  model --> xml["beffroi/xml-security"]

Inside the pure-PHP packages of the provider, the core and the two protocols, the same rule is drawn again, in four layers: Domain holds the model and its rules, Port the interfaces the outside implements, Application the use cases that orchestrate them, and Bridge the implementations that need a library. A static analysis of the dependency graph fails the build when a package or a layer reaches where it should not.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
What Which PHP 8.4 or later, with intl; zip for the bundle; dom, libxml and openssl for the XML of SAML, zlib for its HTTP-Redirect binding Symfony 8.2, for the bundle and the application Database PostgreSQL, through Doctrine ORM Licence MIT, for all eight packages

The cryptography of the tokens and the credentials is not written here. Signatures and encryption of JOSE come from web-token/jwt-library, WebAuthn from web-auth/webauthn-lib, TOTP from spomky-labs/otphp, certificates from spomky-labs/pki-framework, and key management from symfony/key-management. The XML of SAML is the exception, written here on purpose, because no library of the PHP ecosystem reads it safely by construction: the SAML packages say what that buys.

docs.title: Secure by default
docs.text: A provider that can be configured insecurely will be, and the person who pays for it is never the one who wrote the option. So Beffroi has no option to do it wrong: the protections below are properties of the code. There is no insecure_ setting, no compatibility mode, and no global switch.

docs.title: What is always on
docs.text: Rule Why PKCE is mandatory, S256 only plain protects nothing against an attacker who reads the request. A code intercepted without the verifier is useless No implicit flow Tokens in a URL fragment end up in history, logs and referrers No resource owner password credentials grant It teaches applications to collect passwords, which is the habit the protocol exists to break Redirect URIs are compared exactly Prefix and wildcard matching is how an open redirector becomes a token leak iss is in every authorization response A client must be able to tell which provider answered. RFC 9207 Access tokens are at+jwt or opaque references, never an ambiguous shape A resource server must know what it is validating. RFC 9068 No redirect is followed outbound Fetching a client's metadata or keys must not become a request to an address the client chose No boolean from a third party is ever cast A missing claim and a false claim are not the same thing, and (bool) makes them one Every secret string comes from a cryptographic source, every secret comparison is constant time A password is compared against a list of compromised values before it is written A password can be long, varied and still known to everybody. NIST SP 800-63B §3.1.1.2 asks for the list, and what the list holds is refused rather than warned about A password is fifteen characters at least where it signs somebody in alone, eight where a second factor goes with it NIST SP 800-63B §3.1.1.2 makes the length two numbers, and the floor of the logins of the tenant says which one a password serves A page that adds or takes away a way in asks for the proof again A session outlives the moment it was opened, which is right for a page that shows what the account holds and wrong for the gesture somebody else would lock its owner out with What leaves the process on a transport leaves sealed What a column seals, a queue may not carry in clear: the body of every message is sealed to the tenant, so a broker, a failure table and a backup of either are worth nothing without the key management service Every end of a session revokes what was issued under it However a session ends, at the end session endpoint, from the account, by the console or by a SAML logout, its refresh tokens are revoked, its opaque access tokens removed, and the provider refuses every token of it from then on. What a resource server verifies offline, a self-contained access token, lasts until it expires, which is why it lives ten minutes by default A form another site posts a browser to the provider with is posted again from the provider's own origin, and a post from another site is never answered with a new session cookie Under SameSite=Lax a cross-site POST arrives without the session. Answered with a new cookie, it would sign the browser out of the provider; posted again, it reaches the session the browser holds. Both rules read where the post comes from in Sec-Fetch-Site, and a browser that does not send it is answered as it always was A person of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for signs in there and nowhere else A local password would outlive the person's departure from the directory of their organisation, so none is posed for them and none is accepted from them In SAML, every assertion the provider writes is signed, no signature under SHA-1 is accepted, nothing is encrypted in CBC, and no response is taken that nobody asked for SAML 2.0 gives the whole list, and why each rule is there

docs.title: Where an exception exists
docs.text:
An exception is named, bounded and written down, never a switch in a configuration file. Two examples of the shape they take:

  • PKCE can be waived by the registration policy, not by the client. A tenant that must serve a client which cannot do PKCE says so in its own policy, for that client, and the waiver is visible where clients are read.
  • Dynamic client registration is controlled. The endpoint exists, and the tenant decides the mode it runs in: who may register, what an initial access token buys, and which authority may vouch for a piece of software it did not issue.
  • An unsigned SAML request is accepted from one service provider at a time. A service provider that cannot sign its AuthnRequest, as Microsoft Entra ID federating its guests cannot, is declared so, and its unsigned requests are then accepted when its own metadata do not say it signs. Nothing turns the signature off for a tenant or a deployment, and a logout request is signed whatever the declaration says.

The floor of the logins of a tenant is a predicate, and a predicate only ever asks for more proofs: a tenant can require two factors or a passkey of every login, and no floor can forbid the stronger credential or let a login prove less than one factor. A floor that leaves out a kind of credential forgets every credential of that kind rather than leaving it dormant. The floor of its logins says what it changes.

docs.title: Keys and personal data
docs.text:
Signing keys and the data keys that protect personal data are held by a key management service, never by the application: the application asks for an operation and never holds the master key. Keys rotate without a restart and without breaking a token already in flight.

Personal data is sealed in its column, with blind indexes for the lookups that must still work. A dump of the database is searched byte by byte by a test that fails when it finds a value it should not, and the same search finds a value the schema declares readable, so a green run is a search that was looking.

A key works for an age and no longer: a successor is staged behind it without anybody asking, and beffroi:keys:list --check fails on a key that has worked past that age with nothing staged behind it, so the question is answered in a deployment pipeline rather than at the next rotation.

The one file in which everything the provider holds of a person stands in clear at once is the archive that person asks for, and it is held by three rules rather than by a setting: it is sealed where it sits like every other column, it expires a week after it was asked for, and that week is a figure in the code. A person who wants it to leave under a passphrase of their own choosing says so when they download it, and the floor on the length of that passphrase is refused rather than warned about, since what stands between that file and whoever took it is the length of what was typed.

Keys and personal data.

docs.title: What a deployment answers with
docs.text:
Headers are shared by a rule: the bundle writes what belongs to a page it builds, the application writes what belongs to a deployment, and neither writes a header the other does. A header written twice is not replaced, it collides: two content policies intersect, two Access-Control-Allow-Origin are invalid and the response is rejected.

What the standalone application answers with is therefore named where that application is configured and nowhere else: nosniff and DENY everywhere, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, HSTS for a year with the subdomains and the preload list, a permissions policy whose whole set is written down with two entries open to this origin alone, the two a passkey ceremony needs, and a content policy that starts at default-src 'none' and then names one directive per kind of thing a page of this deployment loads. Neither unsafe-inline nor unsafe-eval is one of them.

The one header of that configuration that opens anything is CORS, so it is cut to what needs it: the six endpoints a public client running in a page calls, which are discovery, the JWK Set, the token endpoint, UserInfo, revocation and the pushed authorization request. Credentials are never allowed, which is what makes the wildcard correct: a browser refuses the two together, and the session of this provider is read on pages of the interaction plane, none of which is on that list.

docs.title: The packages
docs.text:
The eight packages share one version number, released together from the monorepo. A minor version has its own maintenance branch, named after it: 0.1, 0.2, then 1.0, 1.1, and so on. A fix goes to the oldest branch it applies to and is merged forward; a feature goes to the newest.

Until 1.0 the public API may change between minor versions, and what changes is written in the migration guide of the version that changes it.

docs.title: This documentation
docs.text:
One branch of beffroi-auth/docs per version of the packages, with the same name. The selector at the top of the page switches between them, and latest points at the newest released version, which is what the root of the site serves.

So a page you read always belongs to a version: it describes what that version does, not what the next one will. A page that is not written yet carries a pencil in the navigation rather than a sentence that sounds true.

docs.title: What is Beffroi?
docs.text:
Beffroi is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, an OpenID Connect provider and a SAML 2.0 identity provider, written in PHP. It is the box that signs your users in, issues the tokens your APIs check, and tells the applications you trust who is at the door. Where an organisation already runs an identity provider of its own, it can send that organisation's people there to sign in, as a SAML service provider.

It comes in three shapes, and you choose one:

  • a Symfony bundle you install in an application you already run;
  • a standalone application, a Symfony skeleton on that bundle, which is the recommended deployment;
  • pure-PHP libraries underneath, usable without Symfony, which is where the protocols actually live.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text: An identity provider has as many reasons to live in the team's own stack as its database does, and none to be somewhere else by default. The protocol knowledge is the job of this project, not of the team that installs it: you should be able to read what applies, replace it, and leave with your users.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text:
Beffroi owns its identity model. It has its own user, its own credentials, its own linked identities, its own groups, and its own tenant, and it never hooks onto the User entity of the application that hosts it. A provider that borrows the host's user model cannot hold a stable subject identifier, cannot hold several kinds of credential per person, and cannot be moved out of the application later.

A person in Beffroi can hold a password, a passkey, a TOTP secret and backup codes at the same time, each one a credential of its own kind, each one revocable on its own. And a person is one person whichever protocol reaches them: a browser signed in by OpenID Connect is signed in for SAML, and a session that ends ends for both.

docs.title: What it refuses to do
docs.text:
The list is short, and none of it is behind an option:

  • no implicit flow, no resource owner password credentials grant;
  • PKCE with S256 only, never plain;
  • redirect URIs matched exactly, never by prefix or pattern;
  • iss in every authorization response, so a client can tell who answered;
  • no redirect followed to a third party, no boolean coming from a third party ever cast;
  • in SAML, no signature under SHA-1, nothing encrypted in CBC, and no response taken that nobody asked for.

Those are rules of the code, not settings of a file. There is no insecure_ option and no global compatibility switch to turn them off. Secure by default says why, and names the few exceptions that exist, each one bounded.

docs.title: What proves it
docs.text: The protocols are judged from outside. The conformance suite of the OpenID Foundation runs against the provider in continuous integration, plan by plan, in the strict mode a certification submission asks for. A green run nobody started is not a result, so the runs that matter are asked for by hand and read. SAML has no certification programme, so it is judged by the implementations it has to work with, SimpleSAMLphp and Microsoft Entra ID among them, and every signature it writes is verified by tools that are not its own. Conformance says which plans run and what they cover.
